articles.title: IndiGo Confirms Lie-Flat Beds on A350s (Nov 2026)
articles.excerpt: At Aviation India 2026 on 2 November, IndiGo's CEO said its first 10 Airbus A350-900s will have 16 lie-flat business seats, with deliveries from Q2 2028.
blocks: IndiGo's chief executive, Willie Walsh, said on 2 November 2026 that the airline's first Airbus A350-900 aircraft will have lie-flat beds in business class, and that its future A321XLR jets will get them too. Two reports published on 3 November describe his remarks at Aviation India 2026 in New Delhi. The A350 deliveries are expected to begin in the second quarter of 2028. This article is based on those reports and is accurate as of 4 November 2026.

**Aircraft:** IndiGo has 60 Airbus A350-900 aircraft on order.
**First ten A350s:** three cabins, with 16 lie-flat business seats, premium economy and economy.
**Delivery timing:** deliveries are expected to begin in Q2 2028.
**Later aircraft:** Walsh said more lie-flat business seats could be fitted to later A350s.
**A321XLR:** future A321XLR deliveries will also have lie-flat business seats.

According to Aerospace Global News, Walsh said the airline "needed to have flatbeds as part of the business class product" because that is what customers expect on long routes. The same report says IndiGo has not yet confirmed who will make the seats, the detailed cabin layout or the amenities.

Business Today reports that IndiGo currently has four A321XLR aircraft, expects one more by the end of 2026, and plans to have 14 by the end of December 2027. The A321XLR is a single-aisle jet with extra fuel capacity for longer routes. According to Aerospace Global News, the A321XLRs flying now use reclining seats under the airline's IndiGoStretch product, not lie-flat beds.

Aerospace Global News also reports that IndiGo will keep operating A321XLR flights to Amsterdam to hold its airport slots before the A350 arrives, and that its London Heathrow service stays suspended until the A350 enters service.
The wider fleet and network plans

IndiGo operates more than 440 aircraft now and expects a fleet of 600 by 2030 (Business Today).
The airline has stopped flying leased Boeing 787 aircraft, citing high fuel prices and airspace restrictions (Business Today).
International capacity is expected to make up 40% of the network (Business Today).
IndiGo reported a loss of Rs 1,879.1 crore for the September quarter, which Business Today links to fuel costs and rupee depreciation.

Walsh also said, according to Business Today, that the short-haul network will not be weakened to support long-haul flying, and that the domestic network can feed long-haul services. He said he is not currently considering fuel hedging, though that may be reviewed as long-haul flying grows.

The reports do not give a launch route for the A350, ticket prices, the exact number of A350s by year, or the seat supplier. Delivery dates for aircraft can also move. The A350 date given here is the one stated at the briefing, as reported, not a delivery contract seen by this site.
Why it matters for passengers and the market

Until now, Indian airlines' long-haul flying has been limited by aircraft and cabins. Business Today reports Walsh saying that only 78 million passengers flew internationally from India last year, fewer than pass through London Heathrow, and that any long-haul opportunity should be based in India. He also said some international flights are moving to Navi Mumbai airport, which he described as in IndiGo's interest. These are statements reported from the briefing, not figures checked against government data by this site.

Aerospace Global News adds that Walsh said the airline will keep its cost discipline and low-fare model while adding the premium cabin. The lie-flat seats are therefore aimed at long routes, where passengers may sleep, and not at IndiGo's short domestic flights. Business Today also reports Walsh warning against being distracted by the excitement of the A350 and neglecting the short-haul narrow-body operation.

On airport costs, Business Today reports that Walsh repeated his view that airport charges and taxes in India are too high and should be lowered. That is his stated opinion, as reported, and the reports do not give any response from airport operators or the government.

Where the facts come from: remarks by IndiGo's CEO at Aviation India 2026 on 2 November 2026, as reported by Business Today and Aerospace Global News on 3 November 2026. IndiGo's own press page was not opened for this article.

sources.title: IndiGo CEO as airline prepares for international expansion, Business Today (3 Nov 2026)

articles.title: What an Aerodynamic Stall Is: Angle of Attack Explained
articles.excerpt: A stall is a sudden loss of lift when a wing's angle of attack gets too high. It is not an engine failure, and it can happen at any speed.
blocks: An aerodynamic stall is a sudden drop in lift that happens when a wing is tilted too steeply into the airflow. It has nothing to do with an engine stopping. Wikipedia states plainly that a stall does not mean the engines have stopped working, and notes that gliders, which have no engine, also stall. What matters is the wing's angle, not the aircraft's speed alone.

NASA's Glenn Research Center defines angle of attack as the angle between the wing's chord line (an imaginary line from the front edge to the back edge) and the direction the aircraft is moving through the air. This angle strongly affects how much lift the wing makes.

For small angles, roughly within 10 degrees either way, NASA says lift changes almost in a straight line with the angle. Tilt the wing up a little more and you get a little more lift. A pilot raises the nose on take-off for just this reason, to increase the angle and make extra lift.

The straight-line rule does not continue forever. At higher angles the air can no longer follow the curve of the wing's upper surface. It separates from the wing and becomes turbulent. NASA explains that this separation of the boundary layer, the thin layer of air next to the surface, is why wings lose lift abruptly at high inclination.

Wikipedia gives a typical critical angle of about 8 to 20 degrees for subsonic wing sections. It varies with the wing shape. NASA adds that the exact stall point is hard to predict by calculation, so engineers usually find it through wind tunnel tests.
Stall speed is a result, not a cause

Because a stall depends on the angle, a wing can stall at any speed. Wikipedia defines stall speed as the speed at which the critical angle is reached in a given set-up, such as a particular weight and flap setting. A heavier load or a steep turn needs more lift, so a higher angle is needed and the stall speed rises. The article says that higher load factors, such as in steep turns, raise the stall speed.

The cure follows from the cause. Wikipedia says that lowering the nose reduces the angle of attack and lets smooth airflow return. It adds that a properly handled stall typically costs only about 20 to 30 metres of height. Pilots train for this under supervision, and this article is general information, not flight instruction.

**Spin:** can develop when one wing stalls before the other.
**Deep stall:** can lock an aircraft in a condition it cannot recover from, typically one with a T-tail and rear-mounted engines.
**Tip stall:** on swept wings, this can cause a dangerous nose pitch-up.

Wikipedia lists several safety devices: stall warning horns, stick shakers and stick pushers, stall strips, vortex generators, washout (a built-in twist in the wing) and angle-of-attack indicators. Their job is to warn the crew or to make the wing stall in a gentler, more predictable way.
Stalls are normally unwanted, but spoilers deliberately break up the airflow to reduce lift. Wikipedia notes this difference.

NASA notes that an airfoil with a non-symmetric shape still makes some lift at zero angle of attack, while a symmetric airfoil makes none at zero. So two wings can reach their stall at different angles and with different lift on the way. For thin airfoils at subsonic speeds, NASA gives the lift coefficient (a number describing how much lift a wing makes for its size and the air's speed) as approximately 2π times the angle in radians, a rule that holds before the stall and not after it.

Past the stall point, NASA says the flow becomes highly unsteady and the lift can change rapidly. For that reason lift charts are normally left blank beyond the stall: the behaviour is hard to describe by a simple line. This also explains why the stall warning devices matter. They tell the crew that the angle is approaching its limit before the wing gives up its lift.
A stall is about angle of attack, not engine power or speed on its own. Sources: NASA Glenn Research Center and Wikipedia, as opened on 4 November 2026.

sources.title: Angle of Attack, NASA Glenn Research Center
